description: Markdown formatting shorthand InputRules: bold, italic, inline code, and strikethrough convert live as the closing marker is typed.

tests.description: Typing '**foo**' in an empty paragraph converts to bold, no literal asterisks remain
Typing '*foo*' in an empty paragraph converts to italic, no literal asterisks remain
Typing '_foo_' converts to italic, same result as '*foo*'
Typing a backtick-delimited 'foo' in an empty paragraph converts to inline code, no literal backticks remain
Typing '~~foo~~' in an empty paragraph converts to strikethrough, no literal tildes remain
Typing '**foo**' straight through never transiently fires the italic rule before bold's closing '**' completes
Backspace right after a '**foo**' conversion reverts it via undoInputRule. The intermediate assertion (conversion happened) guards against a no-op Backspace passing trivially.
Typing '**foo**bar' immediately continues -- the continuation text 'bar' is not bold (no stored-mark carry-over)
Inside an existing code mark, typing '**bold**', '*em*', and '~~strike~~' converts nothing -- markers stay literal, guarding the code-mark-suppression check.
Typing three backticks leaves the paragraph alone; the code block is made by Return.
Return after three backticks at the start of an empty paragraph makes an empty code block with the caret in it and no language.
Return after three backticks and a language makes an empty code block with that language; the fence text does not remain as a first line.
A language containing punctuation, like c++, is kept as typed.
Text typed after the Return lands in the code block, first on its first line.
Undoing the conversion restores the paragraph holding the fence text.
Return after a fence that follows other text in the paragraph is an ordinary Return.
Return with the caret before the end of the fence text is an ordinary Return.
Return after a fence with a space and a word after the backticks is an ordinary Return.

Completing a bold conversion around a range containing a link preserves the link and href -- only delimiters are deleted. Link outranks strong in the schema, so serialization splits <strong> around the <a> instead of nesting it.
Typing '**bold *it* x**' straight through preserves the inner em mark created mid-type. Em outranks strong in the schema, so serialization nests <strong> inside <em>, not the reverse.
Typing 'snake_case_name' does not italicize 'case' -- the underscore rule must not fire intraword, per CommonMark's flanking rule for '_' emphasis.
Typing 'a * b * c' (spaced asterisks, e.g. multiplication) does not italicize -- the em rule's flanking requirement rejects delimiters with a space on the inner side.
Typing '**foo*' and stopping there (bold's second closing asterisk never arrives) leaves the text fully literal -- an odd, unmatched delimiter count must never convert.
